title: The Resplendent Victory of Saarbrück
text:
Emperor in the middle, in an apotheosis

blue and golden: he advances, stiff on the horse,

dazzling, happy, for he sees everything rosy,

fierce as the god Zeus, gentle as a papa;


below, the Recruits, who were taking a nap,

beside golden drums and crimson cannons,

rise, discreetly. Pitou dresses himself

and, turned toward his Chief, so much name bewilders him.


To one side, Dumanet leans on the butt

of the chassepot; his close-cropped neck does not tremble:

"Long live the Emperor!" His neighbor is silent...


A shako rises like a black sun... —In the center

Boquillon, in blue and crimson, naive, from behind his belly

emerges and, showing his ass: "So what?..." he asks.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the mock-heroic military tableau and Rimbaud's comic deflation at the end.

title: Vowels
text:
A black, E white, I red, U green, O blue: vowels,

one day I will tell your latent birth:

black furry corset of dazzling flies,

A, buzzing around atrocious stenches,


bays of shadow; E, candor of pavilions

and ships, proud ice, white kings, umbels

that tremble. I, spat blood, laughter of wrath

on a lovely lip, on a lip drunk with penitence;


U, cycles, divine vibrations, green seas,

peace of pastures sown with animals, of furrows

that alchemy has engraved on studious brows.


O, superhuman Trumpet pregnant with strange

stridencies and silences crossing Worlds and Angels:

O, Omega, violet glow of Her Eyes.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the synesthetic vowel-color sequence and the climactic Omega.

title: Sonnet
text:
You see that

I do not let you go, that I bind myself

to your blond and vaporous memory,

fugitive

in the street and silent,

I, who was power and rapture.

I stretch myself

as far as I can; I doubt and try

to grasp your dress, beautiful because it is yours;

always fitted and at the same time sumptuous,

temptation here and there reserve.

Look at me in

a café in this little square

where traffic crackles and burns in the sun

and where everything, even a streetcar, flies.

I think of

you, of your eyes, of your afternoon...

And I would like to swell like a sail

and I take refuge inside myself, cowardly.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the speaker's attachment to a fugitive memory and the urban café setting.

text:

editorial_note: This alternate catalog title preserves the embedded sonnet heading and duplicate source text.

title: Seeing Herself in a Faithful Mirror
text:
Seeing herself in a faithful mirror,

Lice, now old, and seeing that art

could find no part in her face

without natural ruin,

said: "Mortal beauty,

since mortal was its origin,

although Love himself gives it

his arrows to conquer,

let it live obliged to die,

but to grow old, why?"
editorial_note: The translation keeps Argensola's witty complaint that beauty may die, but need not age.

title: Love, If from the Most Perfect Part
text:
Love, if from the most perfect part

my sun never withdraws its living light,

in vain does Phyllis look at me with pity,

and you kindle your arrow in her eyes.


Not as I did the hero who loved Deianira so much

shine upon Oeta,

nor is Olympus' summit calmer

from the wrath of lightning and winds.


And just as high up there on its height,

when people climb out of religion,

the ashes of ancient sacrifices,


Phyllis will find highly kept

sacred signs of my first love

with serene and pure faith and tranquility.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the learned Oeta/Olympus comparison and the sacred traces of first love.

title: Beneath a Tall Beech Meliboeus
text:
Beneath a tall beech Meliboeus

was carving Phaethon on his staff,

struck by that bolt of Jupiter,

which ended his most lofty desire.


On the other side he paints the ugly case

(after he had threatened the world)

of Pompey, beheaded in the boat

by the work of ungrateful Ptolemy.


And seeing his paintings finished,

he says to the valiant figures:

"My grievances made me a third;


and the world envies you, precious souls,

for since we did not finish great things,

we died in the faith of attempting them."
editorial_note: The translation preserves the pastoral carving of failed greatness beside Phaethon and Pompey.

title: What Merit Aspired, Phyllis, to So Much...
text:
What merit aspired, Phyllis, to so much,

if not by surrendering itself to fortune?

How do you offer me today, by offering yourself

as subject of my humble song?


Already on sudden wings I rise,

for your favor turns me into a swan,

to make against envy and death

a glorious injury and gentle fright.


I will sing how divinity pours into

your beauty the soul, and how it inspires

in all your actions its influence;


and how in your gaze wrath shows

such conformity with clemency,

that I do not know if it threatens or reassures.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the swan transformation and the ambiguous gaze between wrath and mercy.

title: Tagus, Producer of the Great Treasure
text:
Tagus, producer of the great treasure

(if we believe fame), whose sand

is full of sapphires and pearls,

your waters nectar, your sands gold;


you then, swollen by my weeping,

will be witness to my beloved sorrow,

as one subject to what love commands,

seeking life, I adore the one who kills me.


When my little shepherdess on your bank

searches for the shells you cast up as you grow,

and with her white foot touches your shore,


the good you enjoy, flattering water

(for in the end you must kiss it, since you wet it),

you usurp from the office of my mouth.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Tagus conceit and the jealous water that kisses the beloved's foot.

title: You Have Seen, Love, That Not to Rebellious Spirit
text:
You have seen, Love, that neither to the rebellious spirit

of natural affection, nor to the violence

of outward beauty, did my free thought

submit to your obedience;


until with nobler power

reason smoothed my resistance,

and by its authority and in its presence,

my free will swore your servitude.


But although the prison I drag resounds,

and proudly my choice sustains the weight,

it is not heard, or not admitted, or is abhorred.


Adorn the prisoner's merits yourself,

for his naked truth does not deserve

that Cynthia should wish to take hold of the chain.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the paradox of freely chosen captivity and the appeal for Love to adorn the prisoner's merits.
